query: In conventional alloys, loss of toughness has long been associated with grain-boundary segregation and brittle grain-boundary precipitation. By contrast, compositionally complex high-entropy alloys can suppress rapid grain coarsening and deleterious intermetallic formation and have shown favorable strength–ductility combinations and resistance to high-temperature softening and low-temperature embrittlement. These findings do not establish what governs possible toughness degradation in an initially single-phase high-entropy alloy. Under the constraint of retaining a compositionally complex alloy suitable for demanding engineering service, what testable mechanistic hypothesis explains whether and why brittle behavior emerges? Specify a controlled comparison that would distinguish the hypothesis from conventional-alloy expectations, predicted observations relative to the initial baseline, its service and loading boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification outcome.

generation.hypothesis: In single‐phase high-entropy alloys (HEAs), high strain rate shear promotes dynamic grain refinement and partial amorphization at the grain boundaries, producing non-equilibrated, high-energy interfaces that become inherently brittle and are prone to decohesion. This mechanism can cause a transition from ductile to brittle behavior even in the absence of impurity segregation or precipitate formation typical of conventional alloys.
generation.material_initial_state: A coarse-grained, single-phase compositionally complex HEA (e.g., CoCrFeMnNi) with well-equilibrated grain boundaries.
generation.intervention: Subject the HEA to controlled high strain rate shear (e.g., via sliding contact) in an ultra-high vacuum (UHV) environment to minimize extrinsic effects such as oxidation or impurity segregation.
generation.conditions: Tests conducted over a range of temperatures (room temperature to moderate intermediate temperatures) and at a high strain rate where dynamic effects (grain refinement and possible amorphous layer formation) are activated, but below temperatures that would induce significant thermally driven segregation.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of ultra-fine, non-equilibrated grain boundary regions and/or a dynamic amorphous surface layer with elevated high-angle grain boundary energies.
generation.mechanism: High strain rate shear induces rapid grain refinement and partial amorphization at the boundaries. The resulting high-energy, disordered grain interfaces have reduced cohesive strength compared to the initial equilibrated structure, leading to a propensity for intergranular decohesion and brittle failure. Unlike conventional alloys where embrittlement arises primarily from impurity segregation or precipitation, the brittleness here is governed by mechanical breakdown of the refined microstructure.
generation.predicted_outcome: Under high strain rate shear, the HEA will show a marked decrease in ductility with fracture predominantly occurring along grain boundaries that have been refined (or amorphized), as evidenced by intergranular cracking and lower measured fracture toughness compared to the initial coarse-grained state.
generation.baseline: The unstrained, coarse-grained single-phase HEA exhibits good strength–ductility and conventional ductile fracture behavior in the absence of enhanced grain boundary modification.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected to dominate under conditions where high strain rate deformation drives dynamic grain refinement at moderate temperatures. At much higher temperatures where diffusion is significant, extrinsic segregation or equilibrium phase changes might override this effect.
generation.uncertainty: It remains uncertain how the threshold strain rate and temperature interplay precisely to trigger the deleterious grain boundary transformations and whether additional minor phases or solute effects contribute to the observed brittleness.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare identical single-phase HEA samples with a coarse initial grain structure. Subject them to a series of controlled high strain rate sliding tests in a UHV environment over a range of moderate temperatures. Characterize the microstructure before and after testing using TEM and EBSD to assess grain refinement and any amorphous interfacial layers, and perform fracture toughness tests with detailed fractography to determine if failure occurs intergranularly.
measurements: Grain size and boundary structure (TEM, EBSD)
Fracture surface analysis (SEM) to identify intergranular vs. transgranular crack propagation
Indirect assessments of grain boundary energy (if available)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the experiments show that (a) no significant dynamic grain refinement or amorphous generation occurs under high strain rate conditions, or (b) brittle behavior (i.e., reduced fracture toughness and intergranular cracking) is observed without corresponding changes in boundary structure, then the hypothesized mechanism of dynamic boundary decohesion would be falsified.

Since their discovery in 2004,, high entropy alloys (HEAs) have been extensively investigated and shown to exhibit remarkable thermomechanical properties,. Studies of grain-size dependent mechanical behavior are limited,, however, especially in the regime of ultra-nanocrystalline grain size where softening (i.e. inverse Hall-Petch behavior) occurs. Recent work has also shown that these alloys are ideally suited for processing using laser-based additive manufacturing techniques, as they exhibit high phase stability and derive much of their strength from thermal history-insensitive mechanisms like solution strengthening. Although recent experimental measurements of HAGB energy with this same alloy (CoCrFeMnNi) exist, a comparison of this prediction is difficult. Measurements of grain boundary energy are sensitive to thermally-driven grain boundary segregation (and possibly phase separation) of impurities. This value is relatively high for metals,, and may imply a propensity for localized cohesive failure or fracture at the boundaries. Grain boundary decohesion has been recently shown to occur readily for this alloy due to segregation and nanoclustering of Cr, Ni and Mn at elevated temperature, and these failures typically originate along HAGBs and at triple junctions. In the present work there is no significant evidence of grain boundary segregation, and this is reasonable as a negligible increase in temperature is expected for these sliding conditions. This suggests that this alloy may also be prone to grain boundary decohesion without significant segregation and phase separation, i.e., when it is a solid solution.
